claims.text: The baseline alloy is a rare-earth-free high-entropy alloy prepared in a near-homogeneous single-phase state.
Changing the cooling rate or applying post-synthesis annealing can produce controlled nanoscale dual-phase heterogeneity while preserving nominal composition.
A dual-phase rare-earth-free HEA can contain compositionally distinct magnetic regions with different magnetic coupling.
The relevant structural mediator is a nanoscale network of phase boundaries between coexisting magnetic regions.
Chemical disorder creates local regions with slightly different magnetic coupling.
Nanoscale interfaces enable a reversible magnetostructural transition under an applied field below approximately 1 T.
The interfaces lower energy barriers for magnetic-domain reordering.
The interfaces promote efficient phonon transport and therefore rapid heat exchange.
The interfaces reduce magnetic pinning and thereby minimize hysteresis.
Distributed strain accommodation at the heterogeneous interfaces preserves mechanical integrity.
Relative to the homogeneous control, the dual-phase alloy will exhibit a significantly larger low-field magnetic entropy change.
Relative to the homogeneous control, the dual-phase alloy will exhibit a significantly larger adiabatic temperature change.
Relative to the homogeneous control, the dual-phase alloy will exhibit lower magnetic hysteresis.
Relative to the homogeneous control, the dual-phase alloy will maintain or improve heat-exchange rates.
Relative to the homogeneous control, the dual-phase alloy will maintain or improve mechanical stability.
The proposed mechanism applies near room temperature to similar rare-earth-free multi-principal-element alloys at fields up to approximately 1 T.
Rapid quenching will promote nanoscale dual-phase heterogeneity, whereas slow cooling will yield a more homogeneous single-phase control.
